sources.claim: Tennessee's ELVIS Act (signed March 21, 2024; effective July 1, 2024) added a person's voice, including a simulated voice, to the state's right of publicity, with liability for unauthorized commercial use and for certain tools whose main purpose is imitating a specific person.

FCC Declaratory Ruling (February 8, 2024): AI-generated voices in calls count as "artificial" voices under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act, so such calls need the same prior consent and disclosures as other prerecorded calls.

The federal TAKE IT DOWN Act (2025) addresses nonconsensual intimate images, including AI-generated ones; from May 19, 2026, covered platforms must provide a removal-request process and act on valid requests within 48 hours, enforced by the FTC.

sections.title: Apply it

questions.prompt: Do publicity rights work the same in every state?

choices.text: Yes, every state has exactly the same publicity law, written word for word the same way

questions.correct_answer: No; they vary
questions.intro: Coverage varies. Publicity rights differ by state; some protect only commercial uses, some extend after death, some cover voice explicitly. Parody, news and commentary may be treated differently, and courts are still applying older laws to new technology. The safe practice does not depend on the exact rule: get consent to use someone's likeness or voice, label synthetic media, and never create sexual or deceptive content about real people.

questions.prompt: Which practice is safe regardless of the exact rule?
